title: Presentations.AI Review 2026: Slides, Editing, Pricing and PowerPoint Export
summary: A source-grounded review of Presentations.AI covering plans, slide limits, editing workflow, project knowledge, and what PowerPoint export actually includes.
body_markdown:
**Verdict:** Presentations.AI appears well positioned for people who want an AI-first way to draft decks quickly, especially if PowerPoint export matters. The catch is that the value depends heavily on plan limits, credit allowances, and whether your team needs lightweight generation or a deeper presentation workflow. Based on the public pricing material available at the time of writing, it offers a real free entry point, clear export paths, and more advanced features like project knowledge on higher tiers. But if you are comparing it with broader presentation workflows, you should be skeptical of vague AI claims and focus on concrete questions: slide caps, export quality, model access, and how much control your team actually gets after generation.


That is the lens for this review. Rather than repeating generic AI-presentation marketing, this article sticks to what can be verified from the product's public materials and makes clear where the evidence stops.


*Methodology note, checked 2026-08-22:* this review is based on the publicly available[Presentations.AI pricing page](https://www.presentations.ai/pricing) and does **not** claim hands-on testing of output quality, editing speed, template depth, or enterprise administration. Where the site states features, those are reported as product claims from the source. Where practical implications are discussed, they are framed as buying guidance rather than observed test results.


## What Presentations.AI seems to be optimizing for


From the available source material, Presentations.AI is not just pitching itself as a slide editor. It is selling an **AI-assisted presentation creation workflow** with plan-based access to credits, model tiers, export formats, and higher-end features such as project knowledge and presentation refresh.


That matters because many so-called AI presentation tools collapse into one of two weak patterns:


-


They generate a first draft quickly but leave you with poor export options.


-


They promise a full replacement for PowerPoint or Google Slides but are vague about limits, controls, or post-generation editing.


Presentations.AI's public pricing page at least gives buyers something more concrete to evaluate. It specifies:


-


a free Starter plan,


-


a Pro plan with a listed annual monthly price in the US,


-


credit allowances,


-


deck slide limits on Starter,


-


PowerPoint and PDF export,


-


different levels of model access, and


-


higher-tier features including project knowledge and presentation refresh.


That is still not the same as proving day-to-day fit. But it is more decision-useful than generic "make better decks with AI" messaging.


## Pricing and plan limits: the part most reviews skip


If you are evaluating Presentations.AI seriously, the pricing structure is the first thing to understand.


According to the official[pricing page](https://www.presentations.ai/pricing) checked on 2026-08-22:


-


The **US Starter** plan is listed at **$0** .


-


Starter includes **100 credits** .


-


Starter supports decks of up to **20 slides** .


-


The **US Pro** plan is listed at **$20 per month billed annually** .


-


Pro includes **5,000 credits** .


-


The site lists **high-quality PowerPoint export** on Pro.


-


The pricing page also lists **PowerPoint and PDF export** .


-


Pricing can vary by country due to **purchasing-power adjustments** .


This is the practical read on those facts:


1.


**The free plan is real, but constrained.** A $0 tier with 100 credits and a 20-slide cap is enough for exploration, small internal decks, or basic qualification. It is probably not enough to assume unrestricted production use.


2.


**The Pro plan is where export starts to matter more.** If your workflow ends in .pptx, the mention of high-quality PowerPoint export is more important than a vague "download" button. In presentation tools, export quality often determines whether AI saves time or just creates cleanup work.


3.


**Credits are part of the economic model.** Buyers should not evaluate only by monthly price. They should ask how quickly credits are consumed across drafting, revising, and regenerating.


4.


**Country-specific pricing means you need to verify your own region.** That is a good reminder not to copy-paste US pricing into procurement docs without checking.

## Editing workflow: what can be said without pretending to have tested it


One of the easiest ways to mislead readers in AI software reviews is to imply a level of hands-on certainty that the sources do not support. So here is the honest version.


From the pricing page alone, we can verify that Presentations.AI is selling more than one-shot generation. The mention of **project knowledge** and **presentation refresh** on higher tiers strongly suggests the product is designed to support iterative work, not just initial slide creation.


That is meaningful because real presentation work is usually iterative:


-


teams revise messaging,


-


sales decks need updates,


-


brand materials evolve, and


-


presentations get repurposed by audience or stage.


However, buyers should separate **workflow promise** from **workflow proof** . Public pricing language does not tell us:


-


how flexible slide-level editing is,


-


how much layout control remains after AI generation,


-


whether revisions preserve design consistency well, or


-


how reliable large deck restructuring is in practice.


So the balanced conclusion is this: Presentations.AI appears to be aiming at a more durable editing workflow than the average AI gimmick, but if editing control is your make-or-break factor, you still need to validate that directly in your own evaluation.


## Project knowledge and presentation refresh: why those features matter


These two phrases are easy to glide past, but they are probably the most strategically interesting parts of the public plan structure.


### Project knowledge


If a presentation tool offers project knowledge on higher tiers, the implication is that it can work from some persistent context rather than treating every deck as a blank prompt. For teams, that matters more than another "generate slides in seconds" promise.


Why? Because the expensive part of presentation work is often not first-draft generation. It is maintaining consistency across:


-


brand language,


-


company narrative,


-


customer context,


-


product positioning, and


-


reusable proof points.


That said, the source available here does not specify exactly how project knowledge is configured, scoped, governed, or surfaced in the workflow. So the right takeaway is not "this solves team knowledge management." It is narrower: **Presentations.AI is at least signaling awareness of repeatable, context-rich presentation work.**


### Presentation refresh


Presentation refresh is another feature label that sounds small but can be important. Teams rarely create only net-new decks. More often, they update old decks for new meetings, products, quarters, or buyers.


If the refresh feature works well, it could help with one of the most common slide pains: making an existing deck current without manually rebuilding it. But again, this article cannot claim how effective that process is in practice. The public source only confirms the feature is advertised on higher tiers.


## PowerPoint and PDF export: probably the most practical buying question


For many buyers, AI generation is not the final decision point. Export is.


Presentations.AI lists both **PowerPoint** and **PDF** export on its pricing page, with **high-quality PowerPoint export** specifically noted on Pro.


That is important for a few reasons:


-


**PowerPoint remains the default handoff format** in many teams, agencies, and enterprise settings.


-


**PDF export matters** for sharing, approvals, and static distribution.


-


**"High-quality" export matters more than export existence** , because low-fidelity export can erase any time saved upstream.


Still, buyers should be careful not to overread this. The source confirms that export exists and that Pro highlights high-quality PowerPoint export. It does not, on its own, prove:


-


pixel-perfect parity with in-app layouts,


-


how editable exported PPT files are,


-


how fonts, spacing, or complex elements transfer, or


-


whether enterprise brand systems survive export cleanly.


If your process requires a deck to end in PowerPoint for final edits, stakeholder comments, or executive polish, this is one of the first things to validate in a trial. In the broader market, export quality often separates serious tools from demo-friendly ones.

## Main strengths visible from the source


-


**Clearer commercial structure than many AI tools.** You can see a real free tier, a paid tier, credits, slide limits, and export options.


-


**PowerPoint is not treated as an afterthought.** The product explicitly lists PowerPoint export and calls out high-quality PowerPoint export on Pro.


-


**Higher-tier positioning goes beyond gimmicky generation.** Project knowledge and presentation refresh imply a more serious attempt at recurring deck workflows.


-


**Model tiers are acknowledged.** Distinguishing standard, advanced, and frontier model access is more honest than pretending all AI plans are equivalent.


## Main caveats and open questions


-


**Credit economics need scrutiny.** A plan can look affordable until iterative revisions consume credits faster than expected.


-


**Editing depth is not verified here.** Public pricing language is not enough to judge whether post-generation control is excellent or frustrating.


-


**Export quality should be validated for your use case.** Especially if your team depends on editable PowerPoint files for final polish.


-


**Region-specific pricing means the headline price may not be your actual price.**


-


**Higher-tier features are named, not fully explained.** Buyers should ask how project knowledge and refresh work in practice before assuming they solve team consistency.


## How it compares with other ways to make AI presentations


The real decision is usually not "Presentations.AI or nothing." It is which workflow creates the least downstream friction.


If you want a broad overview of the category, start with our guide to[the best AI presentation makers](https://getalai.com/blog/best-ai-presentation-makers) . If your current workflow starts from a language model and ends in slides, our walkthroughs on[using ChatGPT to make a PowerPoint presentation](https://getalai.com/blog/how-to-use-chatgpt-to-make-a-powerpoint-presentation) and[using Claude to create presentations](https://getalai.com/blog/how-to-use-claude-to-create-presentations) show an alternative route. And if your input is already a URL or rough deck, tools like Link to PPT or Prettify Deck may fit better than starting from scratch.


That is also where Alai is relevant for some teams: not as a generic mention, but as a workflow choice. If your pain is less about one-click generation and more about turning messy source material into cleaner presentation outputs, a different stack may be a better fit than a pure AI slide maker.


## Should you use Presentations.AI?


**Yes, probably** if your priority is fast AI-assisted deck creation with a credible route to PowerPoint export, and you are willing to evaluate credits and editing control carefully.


**Maybe not** if your team needs deep design precision, fully proven enterprise controls, or certainty about advanced editing behavior before adoption.


The encouraging part is that the product's public pricing page gives enough structure to make a serious shortlist decision. The limiting part is that no pricing page can answer the practical questions that matter most after generation: how controllable the deck is, how stable exports are, and how smoothly the tool fits into your team's real review loop.


That is the right final frame for Presentations.AI in 2026: **promising and commercially legible, but still worth validating around credits, editing, and export fidelity before you commit a team workflow to it.**
